paras: The lynching of Sam Shelton and Jim Keys took place at Belton, Bell County, Texas, about 1 a.m. on the night of Saturday, May 20, 1882, when a mob of masked men took the two prisoners, one white and one Black, from the county jail and hanged them to a tree. No one in the mob was identified, and an inquest was reported to have found the men died at the hands of parties unknown. Texas papers treated it as a return of the mob rule that had long troubled Bell County.

Sam Shelton, described as white, had been jailed about a week earlier, charged with assault with intent to kill Deputy Sheriff Craswell (given as Cresswell in the Dallas Herald). His younger brother, Carroll Shelton, was jailed at the same time on the same charge. Jim Keys, described as 'colored,' was held on a charge of aggravated assault. Both specials said Shelton had been charged with several crimes but never convicted, and that Keys spent much of his time working out fines on the streets.

According to the Dallas Herald's Belton correspondent, the masked men called at the jail for the jailer, F. King, and when Mrs. King said he was absent they compelled her to give up the keys. About twenty-five of them then went in, broke into the cells and brought out Keys and Shelton. The Galveston News special put the whole mob at about 100 and called it 'organized.'

The two men were carried out of town along the public road and hanged to a live oak standing in its forks, about half a mile from the jail by one account and three-quarters of a mile from the public square by another. Hanging directly over the road, they were found early the next morning; the bodies were taken to the courthouse, where they lay all Sunday.

The Dallas Herald reported no clue to who made up the mob or on what ground the men were hanged. The inquest jury had not reported by May 22; the Brenham Banner later printed a verdict of death 'by the hands of parties unknown,' though it placed the case at Waco, an error the Waco Examiner attributed to confusion with Belton. On May 27 Shelton's brother, named Terrell in that report, was released from jail on a $400 bond. No report of arrests, a grand jury inquiry or a trial of anyone in the mob appears in the coverage.

The Waco Daily Examiner covered the lynching most fully, reprinting the Galveston News special under the headline 'Lynch Law of the Same Old Kind' and following it with an editorial, 'Belton--the old, old story.' The editorial recalled the killing of a larger number of prisoners at Belton eight years before and blamed a 'lawless element' in Bell County rather than the community, lamenting 'this devilish mob domination.' The next day the paper printed 'The Belton Murderers,' in which a former Belton resident said neither man was guilty of any proved crime. A week later it wrote that 'Judge Lynch rules the roost' at Belton.

Even while condemning the mob, the Texas accounts disparaged both victims, calling Keys 'a very mean, impudent negro' and quoting the informant that he was 'a saucy negro' who worked well once taught 'his place.' Outside Texas the story ran as a short Galveston wire under headings such as 'Judge Lynch' and 'Lynch Law in Texas,' in the Press and Daily Dakotaian, the Daily Kennebec Journal, the Wheeling Register and the New-York Tribune, often with the names garbled as 'Holton,' 'Hilton,' 'Halton' or 'Kries.' Later condensed briefs in the Mower County Transcript, the Wood County Reporter, the Crawford Avalanche and the Panola Weekly Star misprinted the town as 'Bolton' or merged the charges, and some said the Black victim 'could well be spared.' The Donaldsonville Chief called them 'Two Texas murderers' lynched at Galveston.

The local Belton specials gave Shelton's charge as assault with intent to kill the deputy and Keys's as aggravated assault, while condensed wire briefs said both were charged with murderous assault on a deputy. The Belton-datelined reports are the better evidence on the charges, names and place.

accounts.gist: An organized mob of about 100 masked men hanged the two men to a live oak over the public road three-quarters of a mile from the square; the inquest had not yet reported.

accounts.label: Former Belton resident (Waco Examiner interview)
accounts.gist: Both men were petty offenders, never shown guilty of a specific crime, and he could not imagine why they were lynched; he said a few armed men could have held the jail.

accounts.label: Wire briefs
accounts.gist: Condensed versions with garbled names and places ('Holton', 'Hilton', 'Kries', 'Jim White', 'Bolton') report 100 masked men hanging a white man and a Black man taken from jail.

framing.detail: Under 'Lynch Law of the Same Old Kind' the Galveston News special reported the hanging plainly but called Keys 'a very mean, impudent negro'.
The Waco Examiner's editorials ('Belton--the old, old story'; 'Judge Lynch rules the roost') condemned 'devilish mob domination' in Bell county while sparing the Belton community.
'The Belton Murderers' (meaning the mob) deplored the lynching through an informant who called both victims worthless and said Keys was 'a saucy negro' who had to be taught 'his place'.
The Dallas Herald's Belton special gave the fullest factual account and noted that no one knew why the men were hanged.
Papers outside Texas ran the Galveston wire as 'Judge Lynch' or 'Lynch Law in Texas', some adding that the Black victim 'could well be spared'.
